author: rti_admin
title: Brutality and Caste: The Murder of Rohit Anil Pathare
content:
What does the recent brutal murder of Rohit Pathare by a dominant caste group show? Here, it is inevitable to know the caste identity of the victim. A young ‘Ambedkari’ man from Maharashtra’s Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar district, and his killing in a hospital after a mob of dominant caste group brutally wounded him, exposes a grim reality of the caste system in India. If we understood it just as an act of violence against an individual, we may miss the social and structural underlying causal factors behind the kind of brutality it witnessed. This is a disturbing reflection of how caste hatred is deeply embedded in the social structure of Indian society, which continues to resurface time and again. This hatred appears at times in the form of Dalit youth like Somanath Suryawanshi, who was subjected to custodial torture and death in police custody, and at other times through incidents such as Khairlanji (2006), Mirchpur (2010), Bhima-Koregaon (2018), and Hathras (2020), alongside countless other cases of caste-based violence that remain unreported.

When a person is dragged out from his own house, in a broad daylight pulled through the streets and brought across a public square; when his wife is kicked in the stomach; when mob directs casteist slurs at him on his caste; when he is tied to a tree in a nearby agriculture field and brutally beaten by an iron rod; when wounds are made on his body by a screwdriver; when stones are used to crush his legs; and when, writhing in agony, he begs for water, urine poured over his face — such an inhuman and barbaric crime cannot remain confined to the individual victim alone. It casts a stain on the claims of so-called civility made by Indian society, the moral foundations of democracy, and the values of humanity at a global level. It also constitutes a grave affront to the universal principles of human dignity and fundamental human rights.

What kind of social system produces such inhuman violence and grants one human being the power to exercise domination and supremacy over another? This question leads us to Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar’s critique of the caste system. In Ambedkar’s intellectual framework, the question of human dignity cannot be separated from the complete annihilation of caste. According to him, caste is not merely a system of social stratification; it is a hierarchical structure of social and institutional inequality based on birth that denies individuals equal social recognition, freedom, and human dignity. Within such a system, caste-based violence does not manifest itself merely through physical assaults. It continuously reproduces through the humiliation of individuals, their systematic exclusion from society, the persistence of different forms of untouchability, and the systematic denial of their equal humanity.

Caste Hierarchy and Relations of Power

The caste system regulates the distribution of human dignity, power, and social rights, creating a hierarchy in which the humanity and dignity of some are systematically subordinated to the social privileges of others. Within this hierarchical order, violence is not merely a form of punishment; it becomes an inhuman lesson intended to remind the oppressed of their supposedly assigned ‘place’ in society. More importantly, caste-based violence cannot be separated from misogyny. When Rohit’s wife was kicked in the stomach by members of the mob, it exposed how caste supremacy employs patriarchy as a weapon of domination. Within the caste system, the bodies of women belonging to marginalised communities are often treated as instruments through which the collective morale of an entire community can be crushed and its members are subjected to collective humiliation.

This hierarchy also exposes a deep contradiction between the equality promised by the Constitution of India and the social inequality of everyday life practices. As long as a marginalised or Dalit individual remains within the conventional social boundaries and silently endures injustice, society appears to have no objection. However, when that very individual takes education, begins to advance, becomes conscious of their rights, and starts questioning the existing social order, the established social mindset becomes deeply unsettled. At such moments, social inequality and casteist arrogance become active forces, attempting to undermine that individual’s confidence and reassert their supposedly assigned ‘place’ in society.

At the same time, this fundamental contradiction highlights the intense conflict between individual morality and caste-based morality, whose most visible expression can be witnessed in the institution of marriage. Here, caste pride, hierarchy, and collective prejudice are often accorded greater importance than another human being’s love, education, suffering, and moral responsibility. This brings to the surface the underlying tension between political democracy and social democracy that Dr. Ambedkar recalled at the constitutional assembly debate. The society that dehumanises its people through caste discrimination and silently tolerates such brutal violence, can it claim to be democratic and civilised? Can it guarantee the meaningful realisation of equal rights to its citizens?

What is the role of the Modern State?

If everyday social relations continue to be governed by hierarchical relations of caste domination and subordination, the political equality guaranteed by the Constitution remains merely formal, and the promise on paper never reaches real lives. If individuals cannot exercise their constitutional rights free from caste-based humiliation, fear, and violence, the constitutional recognition of those rights loses its substantive meaning. Under such circumstances, it becomes imperative to critically examine not only the social order itself but also the so-called welfare-oriented and democratic role of this modern state, which bears the responsibility of intervening in this social order to establish constitutional promises including equality and justice.

A critical assessment of the state cannot be undertaken just because an incident of caste-based violence has occurred. Rather, it must be based on questions such as whether the state took adequate measures to prevent such violence, whether the police acted impartially, whether the investigation was conducted in a timely and credible manner, whether the victims received adequate protection, and whether the perpetrators were effectively held accountable. In other words, the democratic commitment of the state must be evaluated not only through the constitutional provisions it upholds but through its actual institutional conduct in situations involving caste supremacy and violence. When the state falls under the sway of the same dominant ideologies that feed inequality and injustice, instead of confronting them, it stops being the sovereign guardian of every citizen’s equal rights. It runs the risk of becoming one more instrument for reproducing established structures of social domination.

An examination of the functioning of the modern state in the Indian context raises a fundamental question: Do the policies, administrative machinery, police, and institutional practices of the state challenge the caste hierarchy and the socio-ideological dominance of dominant castes, or do they reproduce these very structures in newer forms? This question is not limited to the state’s inaction; it concerns the ways in which different state institutions, their mechanisms, and their everyday practices sustain and legitimise established caste-based power relations. If these institutions had truly been impartial, Rohit’s mother would not have been compelled to pour petrol over herself inside the Vaijapur police station in her desperate pursuit of justice following her son’s death.

That is the grim reality. Despite the existence of the constitutional framework of the Indian Republic, the violent hierarchy of caste supremacy and a kind of violence continues to persist in society through various political, social, and other institutional arrangements, albeit in different forms. Beneath the veneer of constitutional democracy, a parallel, unwritten social law appears to remain operative and is becoming stronger. For thousands of years, this law has sustained caste hierarchies and social domination by continually creating conditions conducive to violence, impunity, misogyny, and institutional complicity. Therefore, the murder of Rohit Pathare must not be understood as an isolated or exceptional incident of violence, but rather as a grave manifestation of the deep-seated conflict between constitutional values and the lived realities of Indian society.

Harshvardhan Ashok Wankhede is a PhD research scholar at the Centre for Political Studies, JNU.

author: rti_admin
title: Class Interests in Casteless Disguise: Can Caste Be Disowned Without Surrendering Property and Lineage?
content:
‘I don’t believe in caste. I have no caste. Let’s build a casteless society.’ One hears this all the time now, from people who call themselves progressive, rationalist, liberal. On the face of it, there’s nothing to argue with. Who could object to that?

But look at the Indian socio-economic structure honestly, and the slogan starts to look less like idealism and more like a sleight of hand. Because you can’t abandon caste in your speech while quietly holding on to the wealth and advantages caste handed you. That isn’t annihilation of caste. It’s a way of protecting the hierarchy while pretending to be above it.

Louis Althusser, in Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses (1970), made a point worth taking seriously here: ideology always exists in an apparatus, in practices—its existence is material. Caste is no different. It isn’t just a mental delusion people can shrug off. It has a material life, and in India that life runs through what we might call PPP: Property, Parents, Privileges.

Property means land, urban real estate, commercial capital—concentrated over generations in dominant-caste hands. Parents means lineage: hereditary prestige, ancestral standing, social capital kept carefully inside kin groups through endogamous marriage. Privileges means the leverage that comes from all of it—the networks that open doors in elite schools, boardrooms, professions, and commerce.

So when someone says they’ve “given up caste” because they dropped their surname, while still inheriting the family estate, the legacy networks, and the generational cultural capital—what exactly have they given up? You cannot disown caste while safeguarding the material lineage and property that caste produced. The two don’t come apart that easily.

Ambedkar: Annihilating Caste Means Annihilating Class

Ambedkar saw this clearly in Annihilation of Caste (1936). The caste order, he insisted, is not some innocent functional division of labour: “The Caste System is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers.”

To the socialists of his day who thought economic reorganization alone would dismantle caste, he put the question squarely: can you have economic reform without first reforming the social order? If that order is graded by caste, what guarantee is there that Indian proletarians—divided into watertight caste compartments—will ever combine against their exploiters?

And on the myth of individual merit, he was blunt: those who benefit from birth, education, family name, business connections, and inherited wealth will win the race. But that isn’t a selection of the able. It’s a selection of the privileged. For Ambedkar, annihilation of caste was never about nominal changes in personal conduct. It demanded structural equality across economic, educational, political, and material life. Keeping the assets inside dominant groups while claiming caste is abolished runs directly against everything he argued.

The Biography of the “General Category”

Sociologist Satish Deshpande, in “Caste and Castelessness: Towards a Biography of the ‘General Category'” (2013), gave this rhetoric its proper name. Upper castes, he showed, have systematically laundered historical caste capital into the secular language of “merit” and individual competence. They shed the overt markers of caste, settle comfortably into the constitutionally unmarked “General Category,” and reinvent themselves as casteless modern citizens.

The burden of caste then gets shifted entirely onto SC, ST, and OBC communities—who are caricatured as “casteist” or backward for invoking affirmative action. Constitutional certificates become a badge of sectarian identity, while upper-caste generational capital passes as unmarked merit. That’s the strategy of the General Category, and Deshpande names it for what it is.

Lately there have been petitions before high courts—Telangana, Madras—asking for a “No Caste / Casteless” column in census forms, school transfer certificates, state applications. These deserve a closer look, because they tend to come in two flavours.

One is misguided cluelessness: well-meaning but politically naive people, from oppressed or liberal backgrounds, who imagine that leaving a box blank on a form dissolves structural violence. It doesn’t.

The other is more deliberate: an upper-caste design to escape structural accountability. If caste disappears from the census and public records, surveys can no longer measure how land, corporate wealth, and state power concentrate in dominant groups. And once it can’t be measured, constitutional claims to representation, reservations, and welfare quietly lose their footing.

For marginalized communities, a caste certificate is not a subsidy or a badge of backwardness. It is a tool for survival, statutory protection, and democratic entitlement. In an unequal society, petitioning to erase caste administratively only dismantles the legal foundations of social justice.

What Genuine Annihilation Would Require

It won’t come from rhetorical denial or blank forms. It requires redistributing material resources—land, productive wealth, educational access, and the employment monopolies built through caste networks. It requires treating affirmative action as restorative justice, not charity. And it requires exposing the performance of castelessness that runs in tandem with keeping Property, Parents, and Privileges intact.

Insisting on being called casteless while sitting on accumulated caste monopolies isn’t an emancipatory program. It’s a defence mechanism for the status quo.

Dr. B. Karthik Navayan is an Advocate and Human Rights Activist

author: rti_admin
title: Building Safe Spaces: Women’s Safety Must Mean More Than Protection
content:
A safe workplace is not defined only by the absence of harassment. It is also a place where women can speak, disagree, seek support, and participate in decisions without fear.

We often assume that organizations are safe places because they have rules, policies, and systems in place. But is that enough? A workplace may have a policy against sexual harassment and a committee to receive complaints, yet a woman may still hesitate to speak because she fears being judged, ignored, or facing consequences. This makes me ask a simple question: what does it really mean for a woman to feel safe at work?

Safety is usually understood as protection from harm, injury, or danger. In a workplace, that includes physical safety and freedom from sexual harassment. But it also includes something less visible: the freedom to express an opinion, raise concern, disagree with a colleague, or ask for help without fear of humiliation or retaliation. A woman may be physically safe in an office and still feel unsafe if she cannot speak openly. For me, women’s safety is connected to dignity. It is about being able to work without fear, but also about being treated as a human being whose experiences, feelings, and responsibilities matter.

Physical safety means being protected from violence, injury, threats and other forms of bodily harm. It also includes a safe working environment, appropriate security arrangements, transport where required and access to help in an emergency. Sexual safety means being free from unwanted sexual comments, gestures, messages, touching, harassment and violence. Everyone should be able to decide what happens to their body and should not have to tolerate unwanted behaviour as part of working life. Economic safety includes fair wages, equal opportunities and the ability to earn a livelihood without exploitation or threats. Social and organizational safety means being treated fairly and respectfully, without discrimination, bullying or harassment based on gender, caste, colour or social background.

Psychological safety is equally important. It means being able to express thoughts, ask questions, raise concerns, share ideas and admit mistakes without fear of humiliation or punishment. Amy Edmondson has described it as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Earlier work by Edgar Schein and Warren Bennis in 1965 also discussed psychological safety in relation to organisational learning and change. The central idea is straightforward: people should be able to speak honestly, ask for help and participate without worrying that they will be mocked, ignored or penalised. Psychological safety does not mean avoiding disagreement or accountability. It means that people can engage in difficult conversations without being degraded or threatened.

Safety should be a basic right, not a privilege available only in certain places or under certain conditions. Article 21 of the Constitution of India protects the right to life and personal liberty, and the right to live with dignity has been recognised as part of this constitutional protection. Yet many women continue to experience harassment, discrimination and fear in daily life. When women do not feel safe, the effects go beyond the immediate risk of harm. They may limit their movements, avoid certain jobs, turn down opportunities involving travel or give up professional goals. Insecurity can affect confidence, mental well-being, economic independence and participation in society. It becomes a barrier to equality and empowerment.

For many women, fear begins long before they reach the office. Roads, bus stops, railway stations, public transport, markets and the route home are all part of the working day. Some think twice before travelling alone, returning late or visiting an unfamiliar place. Some ask a father, brother, male relative or friend to accompany them because they believe another person’s presence may protect them from unwanted attention. Instead of feeling free to move independently, they make arrangements simply to feel secure.

A baseline household survey conducted in Delhi in October and November 2012 offers a stark illustration of this fear. The study, carried out by the International Center for Research on Women (ICRW) as part of the Safe Cities programme with UN Women and local partners, found that only 5% of women and girls surveyed ranked public spaces in Delhi as safe from sexual violence. This is sometimes summarized as 95% feeling unsafe, but it is important to be precise: the finding concerns Delhi, not women and girls globally, and reflects respondents’ perceptions of safety at the time of the survey. The study included 2,001 women and girls and 1,003 men and boys aged 16–49. It also found that 51% of male respondents reported having perpetrated sexual harassment or violence against women and girls in public spaces at some point, while 25% said they had done so in the preceding six months. The study included behaviours ranging from sexual comments, whistling, leering and obscene gestures to flashing, stalking, unwanted touching or groping, and sexual assault. These are historical findings from Delhi and should not be mistaken for current national or global prevalence estimates.

The consequences of this fear can be seen in individual lives. A report on gender-based violence describes Srishti, a 20-year-old student in Delhi, who said she had begun carrying pepper spray when she went out. Her parents had also become more protective, wanting to know where she was going, when she would return, and whom she would meet. Her account captures how the threat of sexual violence can shape not only a young woman’s choices but also the behaviour of those who care for her. Safety concerns can lead families to monitor women’s movements and women themselves to plan around risk, restrict outings or change their routines. These precautions may feel necessary, but they also place the burden of preventing violence on women and their families rather than on those who harass or harm them.

Women are also often told to dress appropriately, avoid certain places, stay home at particular times, or behave in ways society considers acceptable. When harassment or violence occurs, questions are sometimes asked about a woman’s clothing, behaviour, or decisions instead of holding the person responsible accountable. Why should women have to limit their freedom because of someone else’s behaviour? Being born a woman should never mean having to live with constant fear. Women deserve the freedom to travel, work, study, and make decisions with dignity.

Improving safety in public spaces requires more than installing cameras or increasing police presence. Roads and bus stops need appropriate lighting; public transport should be safe and reliable; reporting systems should be accessible; and complaints must receive timely attention. Cameras need to be functional and monitored, and policing must be responsive rather than merely visible. Law enforcement and public awareness matter, as does a culture in which harassment is not tolerated. Statistics can help explain the scale of a problem, but they must come from reliable sources and be interpreted carefully. A survey conducted in one city, for example, should not automatically be treated as representative of every woman across India. The responsibility for preventing violence belongs to those who cause harm, the institutions that must respond, and society as a whole.

The same questions must be asked inside workplaces. An organisation may have a formal policy against sexual harassment, a committee to receive complaints and statements promoting gender equality. These are important safeguards, but they do not automatically make every woman feel safe. A woman may hesitate to report harassment if the person responsible is her manager, a senior colleague or someone with considerable influence. She may fear losing her job, damaging her professional reputation, being blamed or facing further harassment. The effectiveness of a policy depends on how it is implemented and whether women trust the people responsible for enforcing it.

Organisations must ensure that complaints are taken seriously, investigations are fair, confidentiality is respected, and employees are protected from retaliation. Women should know where to seek help and should have reason to trust that their concerns will be addressed. Clear procedures are important, but so is the everyday conduct of managers and colleagues: whether they listen without dismissing concerns, challenge inappropriate behaviour, and avoid punishing those who speak up. At the same time, we should not assume that every organisation is unsafe or that every workplace offers the same experience. Some organisations make genuine efforts to create supportive environments. The real question is whether safety exists in everyday practice, rather than only in policies and public statements.

These responsibilities become especially important when women work in the field. Fieldwork may require employees to travel alone, visit unfamiliar locations, meet different communities, work in isolated areas, or return home late. In some places, immediate assistance may not be available. Women who work directly with communities may need to visit households or spend long periods away from their usual workplace. Even when the work is meaningful and necessary, the surrounding conditions may not always be safe.

However, it would be wrong to say that all fieldwork is more dangerous than office-based work. Risks depend on the nature of the job, location, working hours, available support and the people with whom employees interact. An office can also expose women to harassment, discrimination or abuse of power, while a well-managed field environment may be supportive. The point is not to label one setting as inherently unsafe, but to understand the risks in each situation and respond to them responsibly.

Reporting can be particularly difficult for women in informal or economically insecure jobs. A woman who depends on her income may fear that raising a complaint will cost her livelihood. If complaints are dismissed, if she is blamed for being in a particular place, or if managers protect the person accused, others may be discouraged from speaking up. Silence should never be mistaken for the absence of a problem. Sometimes a woman does not report an incident because she fears the consequences, not because the incident was insignificant. Organisations must provide clear fieldwork protocols, risk assessments, reliable communication, emergency contacts, appropriate transport arrangements and accessible complaint mechanisms. No woman should have to choose between her personal safety and her livelihood.

My own experience at CORO India, a community-based non-profit organisation, has helped me think about safety in a more personal way. I have experienced a women-centric environment in which women make up a large part of the workforce and take an active role in decision-making. Women are not merely present; they can express their opinions, share their experiences, and help shape the organisation’s direction. This matters because representation alone is not enough. Women also need meaningful influence over the decisions that affect their lives and work. I am describing my own experience here, not suggesting that every organisation or every woman’s experience is the same.

For me, CORO India has often felt like much more than a place where people complete their responsibilities and return home. It has felt like a second home, a family and a community where colleagues can become trusted friends, teachers, mentors and counsellors. What makes this experience meaningful is the feeling of belonging: people try to understand one another, listen to each other’s difficulties and offer support during difficult moments. In my experience, people can express sadness, talk about personal concerns and even cry in front of colleagues without feeling that they must hide their emotions. Sometimes a person does not need advice or a solution. They simply need someone to sit beside them, listen patiently, and allow them to speak.

There are small acts of care that make this environment feel different from an ordinary workplace. People try to make time for one another, even when they have responsibilities of their own. Sometimes support is offered through a conversation, a kind gesture or a moment of comfort after a stressful day. Such gestures may appear small, but they communicate that a person is seen and valued. I have also seen an effort to recognise the person behind the work: someone may be dealing with family responsibilities, financial pressures, discrimination or emotional stress that cannot be understood by looking only at their work performance. In such moments, listening and empathy can help a person feel less alone.

This does not mean that emotional support can replace formal safeguards. A caring culture must exist alongside fair policies, clear boundaries, accountability and systems that protect people’s rights. Good intentions alone cannot resolve misconduct, and personal closeness must never become a reason to overlook harmful behaviour. A truly supportive organisation makes room for compassion while taking complaints seriously and ensuring that everyone is treated fairly.

The bond people develop with an organisation can go beyond a job, salary or professional position. When colleagues trust one another, share experiences and offer support, the workplace can become a community in which people feel that they belong. Leaving such an institution may mean leaving behind relationships and a support system as well as employment. For me, this sense of belonging has helped clarify that safety is not only the absence of physical violence or sexual harassment. It also involves feeling emotionally secure, respected, heard and valued.

A woman may work in an organisation with policies against sexual harassment, but if she is afraid to express her feelings, raise a concern or ask for help, can we say that she feels completely safe? Similarly, if women are employed in large numbers but are not allowed to participate meaningfully in decision-making, can we truly call that organisation empowering? Women’s participation should be measured not only by their presence, but also by whether their views shape decisions, whether they can disagree without fear, and whether leadership responds to their concerns.

My experience at CORO India has shown me how an organisation can nurture trust, support, and belonging. It has also reminded me that no single organisation can stand in for the policies, accountability and wider social changes needed to make women safe. Safety is created through everyday actions as well as institutional systems: the way people listen, respond to difficulties, respect differences, challenge discrimination and share power. People do not leave their personal lives at the office door. We arrive at work with our experiences, responsibilities, emotions and challenges. Recognising this does not weaken professionalism; it can make working relationships more humane and respectful.

Ultimately, women should not have to choose between professional growth and emotional well-being. They should not have to sacrifice their dignity to keep a job or hide their struggles to be considered professional. They deserve workplaces where complaints are handled fairly, their voices are heard, their decisions matter and their safety is treated as a shared responsibility. Building safe spaces means more than protecting women from harm. It means creating organisations where women can speak freely, participate in decisions, receive support and grow without fear—places where people are valued not only for what they contribute, but also respected as human beings whose safety, dignity and well-being matter.

Edmondson, Amy C., and Michaela J. Kerrissey. “What People Get Wrong About Psychological Safety.” Harvard Business Review, May–June 2025. https://hbr.org/2025/05/what-people-get-wrong-about-psychological-safety

author: rti_admin
title: A Ballot and the Barricade
content: Quite often, as I stand at the edge of Jantar Mantar and watch a police officer tighten the barricades across the road, I see space. It surprises me, for, like democracy or citizenship or the human right to protest, space is not supposed to be seen. It is not that standing in New Delhi, this capital of monumental avenues, government buildings and carefully cultivated national spectacles, has given me some special ability to see what I had not been able to see before. It is just that, when the police begin deciding where people can stand, how far they can walk and how long they can remain together, space suddenly acquires a very visible grammar. Everything competes with it for visibility: placards, police uniforms, detention vans, commuters searching for an alternative route, journalists trying to document an unfolding confrontation and, of course, the institutions that seem much easier to approach in a textbook than on the street. Light, which can illuminate a public institution, cannot necessarily illuminate the distance between that institution and the people who wish to question it. title: Miss X Versus Late Rekha Waghmare: The Selective Outrage of Telangana Civil Society
content:
In Telangana, the term “civil society” evokes images of principled activism: women’s groups marching for justice, human rights organisations amplifying marginalised voices, and political parties channelling public anger into demands for accountability. Yet this activism reveals a troubling selectivity when the victim belongs to a Scheduled Caste (SC) community, especially a vulnerable migrant labourer. The stark contrast between the high-profile handling of the Miss X POCSO case and the alleged gang-rape and murder of Late Rekha Waghmare exposes what can only be described as caste-driven hypocrisy. Telangana’s so-called civil society functions less as a beacon of universal justice and more as a caste society indifferent, even complicit, when atrocities target SC “untouchable” communities.

The Miss X Case: Swift Action, Political Storm, and Current Legal Position

In May 2026, Bandi Sai Bhageerath, son of Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Bandi Sanjay Kumar, faced serious criminal allegations under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The complaint, lodged on May 8, 2026, by the mother of Miss X, a 17-year-old girl, accused him of repeated sexual harassment, assault, emotional manipulation, and coercive acts over several months at various locations, including a farmhouse in Moinabad.

Desp
